name: Svalbard Museum
funding: A foundation set up by Longyearbyen's council, the coal company Store Norske, UNIS, the Polar Institute and the Governor. The Svalbard budget pays for running costs and the building. FY2023 income NOK 34.9M.
watch: Store Norske, which ended coal mining on Svalbard in 2025, holds a board seat; the museum keeps 10,000 of its photographs.
records_note: Its 2018 to 2028 strategy names the founders and board seats; accounts are filed in Norway's register.

name: Tromsø Kunstforening (Tromsø Center for Contemporary Art)
funding: Main funders are Tromsø Municipality, the Ministry of Culture and Equality and Troms County; projects get Arts Council Norway, SpareBank 1 Nord-Norge's Samfunnsløftet, KORO and BKH money. FY2025 income NOK 5.6M.
watch: A members' association and the oldest art institution in northern Norway; while Muségata 2 is renovated it works from a former care home.
records_note: Names its main funders and project funders; accounts are filed in Norway's register.

name: Museum of the Second World War
funding: A state institution financed by Poland's Ministry of Culture and National Heritage, which appoints its director. In March 2024 the minister replaced PiS appointee Grzegorz Berendt with Rafał Wnuk.
watch: Opened 23 March 2017 in a 23,000 square metre building with a 40 metre leaning tower by the Kwadrat studio; 601,000 visitors in 2024.

propaganda.summary: In April 2017 the PiS government merged the museum, dismissed director Paweł Machcewicz and installed Karol Nawrocki, who altered the exhibition; from June 2024 the new management reversed those changes, restoring the authors' original vision.

name: Museu de Arte Popular
funding: A Portuguese state museum, run with the Museu Nacional de Etnologia by the Directorate-General for Cultural Heritage until Decree-Law 79/2023 passed national museums to Museus e Monumentos de Portugal E.P.E.
watch: In the popular life pavilion of the 1940 Portuguese World Exhibition in Belém; closed in 2003 and reopened in December 2016 after a citizens' campaign.

propaganda.summary: The Estado Novo's SNI opened the museum in July 1948 from the 1940 exhibition's Centro Regional; the SNI managed it directly and its rural ethnographic vision of national identity served António Ferro's política do espírito.

name: Padrão dos Descobrimentos
funding: Managed since April 2003 by EGEAC, the Lisbon city company that runs the municipal cultural venues. The Portuguese Republic holds title to the monument.
watch: The 56 metre slab was remodelled in 1985 with exhibition halls and a rooftop viewpoint; EGEAC's 2025 programme centres on empire and colonial memories.

propaganda.summary: The Estado Novo rebuilt the 1940 Portuguese World Exhibition monument in concrete in 1960 for the Henry the Navigator quincentenary; scholars call it the regime's brand image and a monument of its ideology.

name: National History Museum of Romania
funding: A public cultural institution under the Ministry of Culture (Government Decision 90/2010), financed by state budget subsidies plus its own revenue; the subsidy was 19,490,552 lei in 2024.
watch: Former Palace of the Posts; a restoration of over 100 million euros, on a Council of Europe Development Bank loan, was announced in October 2024.

propaganda.summary: Ceaușescu pushed the museum open in 1972 over specialists' objections. It increasingly served his personality cult: before 1989 ten rooms held the Homage exhibition of gifts to Nicolae and Elena Ceaușescu.

name: Central Lenin Museum
funding: Closed in 1993 by order of the Russian president. The State Historical Museum, a federal museum, took over the collection and the building on Revolution Square.
watch: Part of the building now holds the 1812 Patriotic War museum.

propaganda.summary: Created in 1935 and opened in 1936, the Central Lenin Museum housed the Lenin cult under the Communist Party. Its first exhibit showed Stalin close to Lenin, and Stalin was cut after 1956.

name: Museum of Contemporary History of Russia
funding: A federal state budgetary institution under Russia's Ministry of Culture, funded from the federal budget. It was the Museum of the Revolution of the USSR until 1998.
watch: In the former English Club mansion at Tverskaya 21; the 2022 exhibition NATO, Chronicle of Cruelty drew almost 20,000 visitors in under two months.

propaganda.summary: In April 2022 the museum opened NATO, Chronicle of Cruelty with Defense Ministry trophies from Ukraine; in 2024 it co-wrote the Culture Ministry's guidelines for special military operation exhibitions nationwide.

name: Museum of Norilsk (Muzei Norilska) and PolArt residency
funding: The city museum runs the PolArt residency and holds about 80,000 objects. Nornickel funds its new Arctic Museum of Modern Art in full, RUB 3B of RUB 150B it put into Norilsk.
watch: Nornickel also backs its exhibitions and courses; AMMA, in a former shopping centre, was due to open in 2026.
records_note: No accounts or budget of the museum were found; AMMA's cost is from The Art Newspaper (2021).

name: Patriot Park
funding: Built and funded by Russia's Defence Ministry, which allocated over 20 billion rubles in 2015. Its head Vyacheslav Akhmedov was arrested for fraud in August 2024 with a ministry general.
watch: A 5,414 hectare site with a 3,530 hectare military base, hosting the ministry's Army forum; conceived by Sergei Shoigu and opened from 2015 to 2016.

propaganda.summary: The Defence Ministry created the park in 2015 for military-patriotic education of youth; in August 2023 it displayed Western armoured vehicles captured in Ukraine during the Army-2023 forum, inspected by Dmitry Medvedev.
